summary.text: In the classic Grignard reaction, a magnesium halide reagent carrying a carbon group adds to the carbonyl group of an aldehyde or ketone.
It is important for forming carbon–carbon bonds, and it must be run under anhydrous conditions or it fails.
François Auguste Victor Grignard described it in 1900 and was awarded the 1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work.

facts.label: Discoverer
facts.value: François Auguste Victor Grignard, University of Nancy

facts.label: Required condition
facts.value: Anhydrous conditions, otherwise the reaction fails

items.prompt: A student runs a Grignard reaction in a flask that still has some water in it. What goes wrong?

options.label: The reagent attacks the carbonyl faster than usual
The reagent acts as a base and picks up a proton instead of attacking
Water becomes the nucleophile and joins the carbonyl
The magnesium halide turns into a carbonyl group

items.explain: With water present, the Grignard reagent acts as a base rather than a nucleophile, so the desired product does not form.

items.prompt: A chemist mixes an organic halide with magnesium. What has been made?

options.label: A Grignard reagent, which is not itself a Grignard reaction
A Grignard reaction that makes an alcohol
A carbonyl compound ready to be attacked
A silyl ether that protects an acidic site

items.explain: The reaction of an organic halide with magnesium is not a Grignard reaction, but it provides a Grignard reagent.

items.prompt: In a Grignard reagent, why does the carbon bonded to magnesium attack a carbonyl carbon?

options.label: Magnesium is more electronegative, so carbon turns positive
The carbonyl carbon is electron-rich and pulls carbon in
Carbon and magnesium share electrons equally
Carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, so it acts as a nucleophile

items.explain: Because carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, the carbon attached to magnesium acts as a nucleophile and attacks the electrophilic carbon of the carbonyl group.

items.prompt: A starting material has an acidic site that would ruin the Grignard reagent. What can the chemist do beforehand?

options.label: Add a little water so the reagent adapts
Add extra Grignard reagent to use up the proton
Protect the site by turning it into an ether or silyl ether
Leave the site alone and run the reaction hotter

items.explain: Protecting the acidic site as an ether or silyl ether removes the labile proton from the solution before the reaction.

items.prompt: A chemist wants a Grignard-type reagent that leaves esters, amides and nitriles alone. Which modification fits?

options.label: Adding lithium chloride, making a Turbo-Grignard
Adding cerium trichloride
Adding nickel or palladium halides
Switching to an organocuprate in water

items.explain: Turbo-Grignards are Grignard reagents modified with lithium chloride, and esters, amides and nitriles do not react with them.

items.prompt: Why do chemists disagree about the modern meaning of the Grignard reaction?

options.label: Some say it needs water, while others say it needs none at all
Some count any electrophile with the reagent, others only aldehydes and ketones
Some credit a different chemist, while others credit Grignard
Some count only reagents that were made without magnesium

items.explain: Classically it means a Grignard reagent reacting with a ketone or aldehyde, but some chemists take it to mean all reactions of any electrophile with Grignard reagents.
